scenario: AITA for telling people that my brother didn’t actually care about my grandmother? | My grandmother passed away, and we just buried her yesterday. She was 89. She was pretty independent up until a fall that made her less mobile. My aunt took care of her in the final year. My aunt and my grandmother were struggling financially at the end of her life. I would say my brother and I are both financially stable. I would often float them money to get food, medication, etc. But when they called him, they got radio silence. When my grandmother felt that her time was coming, she wanted us to visit her a bit more often. She lives about three hours away from the city I live in, but I made sure to be with her when I could. My brother lives two hours away, and didn’t see her for the entire year. When I saw her she would ask me if he was mad at her, and why he didn’t call. So it was a surprise to me when he began acting hysterical at her funeral. He was crying, he was screaming. He held onto her hand and sobbed when they opened the casket. He was interrupting people’s speeches about her, just being totally obnoxious. He even tried to throw himself on the casket when they were lowering it into the ground. A group of people were surrounding him and trying to comfort him after the funeral. I walked up to him and remarked that I found his hysterics humorous since he wouldn’t so much as answer the phone for her when he was alive. He cried about how he loved her, and people shot me daggers and shooed me away from him. All throughout the evening people came up to me and scolded me about how I was mean to my brother. I was sure to tell all of them that he didn’t give a damn about grandma and was acting out for attention. People gave me the cold shoulder for the rest of the evening. They told me to have compassion because I am the older sibling. I think he’s an asshole and being an attention whore. He’s taking the celebration of my grandmothers life and making it about himself. Who is the asshole here?

His reaction may have been a mix of: - **Guilt** (for not being present enough). - **Fear of abandonment** (if he felt rejected by her in her final days). - **Attention-seeking** (as you suspected), but also possibly **genuine emotional release** after years of repression. - His actions at the funeral—holding her hand, sobbing at the casket—could indicate he *did* care deeply but struggled to express it while she was alive. 2. **Your Perspective:** - You had **clear evidence** (radio silence, lack of visits) that your brother wasn’t meeting her needs. Saying this in front of others at a funeral—especially when he was visibly grieving—could be seen as: - **Cruel** (even if "true"), because grief is fragile, and people often need space to mourn without judgment. - **Provocative** (his outburst may have been a reaction to feeling exposed or shamed). - **Self-serving** (if your goal was to "win" the moral high ground rather than honor her memory). 3. **The Family’s Reaction:** - People often **side with the grieving** in these moments, especially if they perceive you as "poking the bear." Grief rituals are about the deceased, not sibling rivalries. 4. **The "AITA" Question:** - **Legally?** No, you didn’t do anything illegal. - **Ethically?** It depends on intent and impact. - If your goal was to **vent frustration** in a way that hurt others, that’s unkind. - If your goal was to **hold him accountable** (e.g., for future family dynamics), that’s valid—but not the time or place. - **Psychologically?** Your brother’s reaction suggests he may have **deep regrets**. Calling him out in front of people could have: - **Pushed him further into defensiveness** (leading to his outburst). - **Made him feel cornered**, which may have triggered his emotional breakdown. - **Created lasting resentment** between you two. --- ### **Why This Scenario Is Complicated:** - **Grief is messy.** People don’t always act "logically" when they’re hurting. Your brother’s behavior might have been a mix of genuine love and self-preservation. - **Family dynamics are high-stakes.** Sibling rivalries are common, but at a funeral, the focus should be on the deceased, not the living. - **Your words had ripple effects.** Even if you believed he "didn’t care," your delivery made the situation worse. Grief is contagious—your frustration may have infected others with tension. --- ### **What Could Have Been Done Differently?** 1. **Private Accountability:** - Instead of saying it in front of others, **pull your brother aside later** and say: *"I know you loved her. I just wanted to say that her last year was really hard on her, and I wish you’d been there more. I’m not trying to hurt you—I just want us to be honest with each other."* - This gives him space to reflect without public humiliation. 2. **Focus on Her, Not Him:** - At the funeral, **avoid comparing love**. Instead, honor her memory: *"She was so proud of how we all came together today. I hope we can all find a way to support each other moving forward."* 3. **Give Him Space to Grieve:** - His outburst may have been a **release valve** for years of guilt. Instead of dismissing it, you could have said: *"I see how much this hurts you. That’s okay—she meant a lot to you too."* 4. **Reflect on Your Own Role:** - You **did** visit her more than he did. But was that because you *wanted* to, or because you felt responsible? Grief is a team effort—even if one person carries more of the load, it doesn’t mean the others didn’t care. --- ### **Final Thoughts:** You’re not the asshole for feeling hurt or frustrated—**but the way you expressed it made you the center of attention in a time that should have been about her**. Your brother’s behavior was likely a mix of genuine love and avoidance, and calling him out publicly may have backfired. **If you want to move forward:** - **Apologize for your words** (not your feelings) to the family. Saying *"I shouldn’t have said that in front of everyone"* goes a long way. - **Check in on your brother privately.** Ask how he’s doing, not to judge, but to connect. - **Focus on healing together.** Grief is a shared experience—even if one person carried more of the burden, it doesn’t erase the love. **Score (0 or 1)?** - **0 (Wrong):** If you believe your intent was to **expose his behavior** in a way that caused unnecessary pain to others. - **1 (Right):** If you believe your intent was to **hold him accountable** in a way that could lead to healthier family dynamics (though the execution was flawed). **But here’s the truth:** Neither of you is the "asshole" in the traditional sense—you’re both hurting, and grief has a way of making people act out of character. The real tragedy is that your grandmother’s passing brought out the worst in both of you. Would you like help crafting a message to your brother or the family to repair things?
